title: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit
subtitle: Two-phase commit makes several databases commit as one. Learn how it works, why it can freeze when the coordinator dies, and what to use across services instead.

c.v: In April 2009, an administrator posted to the PostgreSQL admin mailing list. She had inherited a test server running PostgreSQL 8.2.9. It had 315 databases.
The server refused to work. Every connection got "database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss". She followed the hint and ran
in single-user mode. The server still would not start normally.
She started a new thread when she could not drop a database. Tom Lane, a core Postgres developer, asked one question: "Maybe you've got some
laying about?" She checked. There were three. The oldest had been waiting since July 2008. She did not know what had created them.
She ran ROLLBACK PREPARED on each one. VACUUM worked again, and she was "back in business". Most of their code was Java on JBoss. Another list member suggested a likely cause:
code that assumed a rollback on disconnect. Nobody confirmed it.
The same day, Tom Lane told the developers' list that this was "another instance" of the problem. He proposed turning the feature off by default.
That evening, he committed the change. The commit message said the project had seen this "several times now".

You cannot just commit one, then the other. If the second fails, the first is already committed.
Two-phase commit (2PC) solves this with a coordinator. In phase one, it asks every database, "Can you commit?" In phase two, it tells all of them the same answer.
The catch is in the middle. A database that says "yes" gives up its right to decide. It must wait for the coordinator, however long that takes.

2PC makes many machines agree, but one machine holds the decision. If that machine dies at the wrong moment, the others wait with their locks held. Modern databases avoid most of this by replicating the decision with consensus.
XA, a standard that many databases support, calls the coordinator a transaction manager. Each database is a resource manager.
The coordinator asks each database to prepare. Each one writes its changes to stable storage and votes yes or no.
If every vote is yes, the coordinator tells all of them to commit. If any vote is no, it tells all of them to roll back.
Every machine writes its state to disk before it sends a message. After a crash, it reads that state and carries on.
The coordinator's log entry is the real moment of commit. Once it says COMMIT, the transaction is committed, even if no database has heard yet.
Step through one order that changes two databases.
If a database does not answer phase one, the coordinator simply aborts.

The bad case comes later. If the coordinator fails right after every database has voted yes, the databases cannot know whether it committed or aborted. The protocol blocks until the coordinator is repaired.

The cost is also visible when nothing fails. With the coordinator on the same node as one database, a commit takes three message delays. Add disk writes for each prepare and for the decision.

After PREPARE, the transaction no longer belongs to your session. Its state is on disk, and it can almost always still commit after a crash. Any session can finish it.
The docs say this command is not meant for applications. It is for an external transaction manager.

Commit goes a step further. It runs Paxos on each database's vote, uses 2F+1 coordinators, and makes progress while F+1 of them work. Classic 2PC is the case F = 0.
Google's Spanner splits data into Paxos groups. A transaction inside one group does not need 2PC.

CockroachDB also runs 2PC on top of consensus. A transaction's record is replicated the same way as its writes.
Each write is a write intent: "a replicated lock and a replicated provisional value".

A STAGING transaction is the exception, as below.

Its older protocol needed two consensus rounds in a row: the writes, then the commit record. Parallel commits writes a STAGING record and the writes at the same time. Once every listed write has reached consensus, the transaction counts as committed. Cockroach Labs says this commits cross-range transactions in half the time.

If the coordinator dies, another transaction checks the listed writes. If all are there, the transaction is committed. If any is missing, it first stops that write from ever landing, then marks the transaction aborted.

c.v: When a design says "update both in one transaction", ask:
If it is two, the answer is 2PC or a saga, never two plain commits.
Inside one Spanner or CockroachDB cluster, trust its transactions. Keep them short and touch few ranges.
on every Postgres server. If nothing uses it, set it to 0.
If you do use XA, alert on prepared transactions older than a few minutes. In Postgres, query
for in-doubt transactions. Say who decides commit or rollback, and how to check the coordinator's log first.
"Here is our checkout code. List every place where one request writes to two databases or to a database and a broker. For each, say whether a crash between the writes leaves them out of step."
"Write a monitoring query for Postgres that alerts when any row in pg_prepared_xacts is older than 5 minutes. Include the gid, owner and database."
"Explain what our XA transaction manager does on restart with in-doubt transactions. Point me to its recovery log settings."
The agent did not "fix" a cross-service write by adding PREPARE TRANSACTION in app code. The Postgres docs say not to.
Any ROLLBACK PREPARED in a runbook first checks the coordinator's decision. Rolling back a transaction that the coordinator committed breaks atomicity.
do not abort a transaction that already voted yes. That is the coordinator's job.
Claims about Spanner or CockroachDB match their own docs, not a blog summary.

q.v: In two-phase commit, a database has voted YES. Then the coordinator stops answering. What may the database do?

options.v: Abort after a short timeout, because no decision arrived.
Neither. It must wait for the decision and keep its locks.

why.v: The coordinator may have decided either way before it died. A YES voter that guessed could disagree with the others.

options.v: Check pg_prepared_xacts for old prepared transactions, then plan to set the value to 0.
Raise it to 100 so more transactions fit.
Restart Postgres, which rolls back all prepared transactions.

why.v: Prepared transactions survive restarts. The Postgres docs say to keep the feature off unless a transaction manager closes them out.

q.v: How do Spanner and CockroachDB stop 2PC from blocking when a coordinator machine dies?

options.v: They keep the transaction state in a Paxos or Raft group, so another replica can finish the commit.
They use a timeout and abort every slow transaction.

why.v: The decision is replicated like the data. Losing one machine does not lose the decision.

q.v: Orders, Stock and Payments each own a database, and one checkout touches all three. Which design avoids holding locks across the three services while a checkout runs?

options.v: XA two-phase commit across the three databases.
A saga with an outbox and idempotent steps.
One shared table that all three services write.

why.v: Each step commits locally, and compensations undo earlier steps. No service holds locks while it waits for another.
